questions.question: Can you explain why the converse to Theorem 4 is true, i.e., why does the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord of the circle bisect the chord? (Hint: Use Fig. 5.12. You are told that $\angle CMA = \angle CMB = 90°$. You need to show that $AM = BM$.)

solution.content: **Set up:** Let $AB$ be a chord of a circle with centre $C$. Let $CM$ be the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$, meeting $AB$ at $M$. We are given $\angle CMA = \angle CMB = 90°$.
**Compare the triangles $\triangle CMA$ and $\triangle CMB$:** $CA = CB$ (both radii), $CM$ is common, and $\angle CMA = \angle CMB = 90°$.
**Apply RHS congruence:** By the RHS congruence rule, $\triangle CMA \cong \triangle CMB$.
**Conclusion:** Corresponding sides are equal, so $AM = BM$. Hence the perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord.

questions.answer: By RHS congruence, ΔCMA ≅ ΔCMB, so AM = BM.

formulaBox.title: Theorem 5
formulaBox.content: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord.

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** This is Theorem 5. The perpendicular from the centre to a chord bisects the chord, and the line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it.

diagram.caption: Fig. 5.12: The perpendicular CM from the centre C to chord AB meets AB at M. By RHS congruence, ΔCMA ≅ ΔCMB, so AM = BM — the perpendicular bisects the chord.

geometry.title: Perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord
geometry.description: A circle with centre C and chord AB. The perpendicular CM from C to AB meets AB at M. Triangles CMA and CMB are congruent by RHS, so AM = BM.

questions.question: An isosceles triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle, with $AB = AC$. Show that the altitude from $A$ to $BC$ passes through the centre of the circle.

solution.content: **Set up:** Let $O$ be the centre of the circle. Since $AB = AC$, the chords $AB$ and $AC$ are equal.
**Equal chords are equidistant from the centre:** By Theorem 6, equal chords are at the same distance from the centre. So $O$ is equidistant from the chords $AB$ and $AC$.
**Locate $O$:** The point equidistant from the lines $AB$ and $AC$ lies on the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$. So $O$ lies on the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$.

**Use the isosceles property:** In an isosceles triangle with $AB = AC$, the angle bisector of $\angle A$ is also the altitude from $A$ to $BC$. Hence the altitude from $A$ to $BC$ passes through $O$, the centre of the circle.

questions.answer: O lies on the angle bisector of ∠BAC, which is also the altitude in an isosceles triangle, so the altitude passes through the centre.
questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** In an isosceles triangle, the angle bisector, median and altitude from the apex all coincide.

diagram.caption: Fig. 5.16: Isosceles triangle ABC (AB = AC) inscribed in a circle with centre O. The altitude from A to BC passes through O.

geometry.title: Isosceles triangle inscribed in a circle
geometry.description: Isosceles triangle ABC with AB = AC inscribed in a circle with centre O. The altitude from A to BC passes through O.

questions.question: Two parallel chords of lengths 6 cm and 8 cm are on opposite sides of the centre of a circle. If the radius of the circle is 5 cm, find the distance between the midpoints of the chords.

solution.content: **Chord of length 6 cm:** Its half-length is $3$ cm. Distance of this chord from the centre: $$d_1 = \sqrt{5^2 - 3^2} = \sqrt{25 - 9} = \sqrt{16} = 4 \text{ cm}$$
**Chord of length 8 cm:** Its half-length is $4$ cm. Distance of this chord from the centre: $$d_2 = \sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = \sqrt{25 - 16} = \sqrt{9} = 3 \text{ cm}$$
**Add the distances:** The chords are on opposite sides of the centre, so the distance between their midpoints is the sum: $$d_1 + d_2 = 4 + 3 = 7 \text{ cm}$$

questions.answer: The distance between the midpoints of the chords is 7 cm.

formulaBox.title: Distance of a Chord from the Centre

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** For chords on opposite sides of the centre, add the distances; for chords on the same side, subtract them.

diagram.caption: Fig. 5.17: Two parallel chords AB (6 cm) and CD (8 cm) on opposite sides of the centre O of a circle of radius 5 cm. The distance between their midpoints is 4 + 3 = 7 cm.

geometry.title: Two parallel chords on opposite sides of the centre
geometry.description: A circle of radius 5 cm with two parallel chords AB (6 cm) and CD (8 cm) on opposite sides of the centre O. Their distances from the centre are 4 cm and 3 cm.
